vignette:
Anna is nineteen. She is a dancer. She has been dancing since she was four, and it has always been the one place she felt safe and in control—the studio, the mirror, the way her body knows exactly what to do when the music starts. But now, when she walks into the rehearsal space, she feels like she is standing in a room full of smoke.

It happened eight months ago, on a Friday night in late winter. She was performing in a small club downtown, a contemporary piece with two other dancers. The place was packed. Halfway through the second set, someone smelled gas. Then someone yelled. Then the back wall lit up like a curtain of fire. She remembers the sound—not the explosion, but the screaming. She remembers the heat pressing against her back as she ran. She remembers a man in a red jacket pushing her toward the emergency exit, and then the crush of bodies, the way the air turned thick and black, and the taste of ash in her mouth for days afterward. She got out. Sixteen people did not.

Now she wakes up three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, her heart pounding so hard she can feel it in her teeth. Sometimes she sees the fire. Sometimes she sees the man in the red jacket, but his face is melting. She does not tell anyone this. She lives alone in a small apartment above a laundromat, and she has not been back to a club or a crowded bar since that night.

Her therapist—she started seeing someone two months ago, after her boss said she was missing too many rehearsals—wrote down a score of 76 on some form. Anna does not know what that means. She only knows that she cannot breathe when the house lights dim. She only knows that she stopped taking the subway because the tunnels feel too much like that hallway. She walks everywhere now, even in the rain, even if it takes an hour. Her feet hurt all the time.

At the studio, she gets through the warm-up by staring at a single spot on the floor. She does not look at the other dancers. She does not look at the fire alarm on the wall. When the music swells too loud, her hands start to shake, and she has to stop and pretend she is checking her shoelaces. Her choreographer, a patient man named Lars, keeps asking if she wants to talk. She says she is fine. She says she just needs more sleep. But she cannot sleep. When she closes her eyes, she smells the gas again.

She has not told anyone the full story. She told the police once, and then she told her mother, but her mother cried so much that Anna decided it was easier to say nothing. Now she tells herself that the fire was not that bad. She tells herself that she is lucky, that she got out, that sixteen people did not. But the guilt sits in her chest like a stone. She replays the exit door in her head a hundred times a day: she was the third person out. She could have turned back. She did not.

Last week, she tried to go to a small café with a friend from the company. The friend ordered coffee. The gas burners on the stovetop were blue. Anna stared at them, and then she started to cry. She could not explain why. She left before the coffee came.

She still dances. It is the only thing she knows how to do. But the joy is gone. When she moves, it feels mechanical, like a body going through steps that used to mean something. She cannot feel the music anymore. Sometimes she wonders if the fire burned something out of her that will never come back. She is nineteen years old, and she is so tired.
